props.title: Don't Look Now... We're Being Shot At!

sections.content: La Grande Vadrouille (1966) - known in English as "Don't Look Now... We're Being Shot At!" - stands as France's highest-grossing film for over 40 years until Titanic (1997) dethroned it. This WWII comedy masterpiece pairs French legends Bourvil and Louis de Funès as unlikely heroes helping British airmen escape Nazi-occupied Paris. Director Gérard Oury crafted a perfect blend of slapstick and wartime tension, establishing a template for French comedy that influenced films like La Cage aux Folles (1978) and The Visitors (1993).

sections.content: The film's massive success sparked a golden age of French comedy, particularly for Louis de Funès who became France's most bankable star. His exaggerated facial expressions and manic energy contrasted perfectly with Bourvil's more understated everyman persona. This dynamic influenced countless European comedy duos and can be seen echoed in films like Les Compères (1983) and The Dinner Game (1998).

The film's genius lies in how it handles serious subject matter - Nazi occupation - through comedy without trivializing the historical context. This delicate balance influenced later war comedies like Life Is Beautiful (1997) and Jojo Rabbit (2019). The elaborate chase sequences and physical comedy set pieces were groundbreaking for their time, requiring massive coordination across Paris locations. SUBHEAD: Impact on French Cinema

sections.content: La Grande Vadrouille (1966) established a distinctly French approach to big-budget comedy that emphasized elaborate set pieces and physical comedy. This influence can be traced through The Tall Blond Man with One Black Shoe (1972) to modern French blockbusters like Welcome to the Sticks (2008) and The Intouchables (2011).
